concepts.title: Accidental Cameras

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: The world is full of accidental cameras that create faint images often ignored by the naive observer.
concepts.content:
For an image to appear, we need some way of restricting the rays that hit a wall so that each location only receives rays from specific directions. While the pinhole camera is one way of forming a picture, in most settings, light rays are restricted by accidental surfaces present in the space, such as other walls, ceilings, floors, or obstacles. For instance, in a room where light rays enter via a window, some rays are blocked. Generally, the lower part of a wall will see the top of the world outside the window, while the top part of the wall will see the bottom part of the world outside. As a consequence, most walls will appear as having a faint blue tone on the bottom because they reflect the sky.

(see figure: A wall might contain a picture of the world after all.)

(see figure: Turning the room into a pinhole camera by closing most of the window helps to focus the picture that appears in the wall.)

The world is full of accidental cameras that create faint images often ignored by the naive observer.
concepts.motivation_md: Explains why we don't see clear images on every surface despite light being everywhere. It introduces the concept of light restriction as the fundamental requirement for image formation, showing that 'cameras' can occur naturally and unintentionally in any environment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Images require restricting light rays so each point on a surface receives light from a specific direction.
 - Accidental surfaces like windows and walls can act as crude apertures, creating faint, often unnoticed projections.
 - Closing a window to a small opening can turn an entire room into a functional pinhole camera.

concepts.title: World Coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: World coordinates define a 3D position relative to the camera's pinhole as the origin.
concepts.content: In a World Cartesian coordinate system, the origin is defined as the camera's pinhole. The coordinates of a 3D position of a point, $\mathbf{P}$, in the world are given by $\mathbf{P} = (X, Y, Z)$. In this system, the $Z$ axis is perpendicular to the camera's sensing plane (projection plane).
concepts.motivation_md: Provides a standard reference frame to describe the physical location of objects in 3D space relative to the imaging device.
concepts.recap_md:
- The origin $(0,0,0)$ is located at the camera's pinhole.
 - The $Z$ axis is oriented perpendicular to the sensing plane.
 - A point $\mathbf{P}$ is represented by coordinates $(X, Y, Z)$.

key_passage.text: Let the origin of a World Cartesian coordinate system be the camera's pinhole. The coordinates of 3D position of a point, P, in the world will be P = (X, Y, Z), where the Z axis is perpendicular to the camera's sensing plane (projection plane).

concepts.title: Camera Coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: The virtual camera plane provides a radially symmetric projection in front of the pinhole to avoid image inversion.
concepts.content: The camera projection plane is located behind the pinhole at a distance $f$ from the origin. Let the coordinates in the camera projection plane, $x$ and $y$, be parallel to the world coordinate axes $X$ and $Y$ but in opposite directions. For simplicity, it is useful to create a virtual camera plane that is radially symmetrical to the projection plane with respect to the origin and placed in front of the camera. This virtual camera plane creates a projected image without the inversion of the image. The coordinates in the virtual camera plane have the same sign as the world coordinates, meaning the $x,y$ coordinates are identical to the projection plane apart from a flip.
concepts.motivation_md: Used to simplify the mathematical modeling of cameras by removing the negative signs associated with the inverted image formed behind a pinhole.
concepts.recap_md:
- The physical projection plane is at distance $f$ behind the pinhole and inverts the image.
 - A virtual camera plane is placed at distance $f$ in front of the pinhole to avoid inversion.
 - Virtual coordinates $(x, y)$ share the same signs as world coordinates $(X, Y)$.

For simplicity, it is useful to create a virtual camera plane that is radially symmetrical to the projection plane with respect to the origin and it is placed in front of the camera. This virtual camera plane will create a projected image without the inversion of the image.

concepts.title: Image Coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: Image coordinates are typically measured in pixels and relate to camera coordinates via an affine transform.
concepts.content: Image coordinates, denoted as $(n,m)$, are typically measured in pixels. Both the camera coordinate system $(x,y)$ and the image coordinate system $(n,m)$ are related by an affine transform.
concepts.motivation_md: Bridges the gap between continuous geometric projections (in meters or mm) and the discrete pixel grid used by digital sensors.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image coordinates $(n, m)$ are usually expressed in pixel units.
 - They are derived from camera coordinates $(x, y)$ through an affine transformation.
 - This system represents the final 2D data captured by a digital sensor.

key_passage.text: **Image coordinates**, shown in , are typically measured in pixels. Both the camera coordinate system $(x,y)$ and the image coordinate system $(n,m)$ are related by an affine transform as we will discuss later.

concepts.title: Perspective Projection

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: Perspective projection uses similar triangles to map 3D world points to 2D image coordinates.
concepts.content:
If the distance from the sensing plane to the pinhole is $f$, similar triangles provide the following relations:

$$\begin{align} x &= f \frac{X}{Z} \end{align}$$

$$\begin{align} y &= f \frac{Y}{Z} \end{align}$$

These are called the perspective projection equations. Under perspective projection, distant objects become smaller through the inverse scaling by $Z$. These equations apply not just to pinhole cameras but to most lens-based cameras and human vision as well. The notion of similar triangles, introduced by Thales of Miletus around 624 B.C., serves as the geometric foundation for these derivations.
concepts.motivation_md: Provides the fundamental mathematical model for how 3D scenes are mapped onto 2D surfaces, capturing the essential property that distant objects appear smaller.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perspective projection is governed by the equations $x = f(X/Z)$ and $y = f(Y/Z)$.
 - The model relies on the geometry of similar triangles.
 - Objects undergo inverse scaling by their distance $Z$, causing them to appear smaller as they move away.

key_passage.text: Under perspective projection, distant objects become smaller, through the inverse scaling by Z. As we will see, the perspective projection equations apply not just to pinhole cameras but to most lens-based cameras, and human vision as well.

concepts.title: Soda Straw Camera

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: A soda straw camera uses parallel tubes to create an orthographic projection where object size is independent of distance.
concepts.content: A soda straw camera is a device designed to achieve orthographic projection by restricting light rays so that only those perpendicular to the plane illuminate the sensor. It consists of a set of parallel straws that allow parallel light rays to pass from the scene to the projection plane while extinguishing rays from other directions. The effect is improved if the straws are painted black to reduce internal reflections. Unlike a pinhole camera, the soda straw camera does not invert the image, and objects do not get smaller as they move away. The resulting image projection is orthographic with a unity scale factor; object sizes on the projection plane are identical to their sizes in the world.
concepts.motivation_md: Demonstrates an alternative to perspective projection, creating an image where parallel lines in the world remain parallel and object size is preserved regardless of depth.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses parallel straws to filter out all but perpendicular light rays.
 - Produces an orthographic projection with a unity scale factor.
 - Does not invert the image or scale objects based on distance $Z$.

key_passage.text: A set of parallel straws allow parallel light rays to pass from the scene to the projection plane, but extinguish rays passing from all other directions.
